Attendees (recorded): Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Narayanan (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (Redwood Marketing), Emma Ortiz (CTO, BlueNova), Samir Patel (Lead ML Eng, BlueNova), Lucia Gomez (Head of Product, BlueNova)
summary: A lightly structured customer marketing interview recorded as a podcast-style conversation. BlueNova Labs discusses their migration to Redwood Inference for production LLM features, the operational and cost outcomes, and what surprised them during the onboarding. Conversation covers latency improvements, dedicated capacity tradeoffs, SOC 2 and data residency concerns, and customer-suggested messaging for the case study. No heavy legal/technical deep dive — more focused on customer outcomes and soundbites for marketing.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Jordan from Redwood. How are we doing?
[00:06] Emma: Hey! Doing good, thanks. Happy to be here, bit weird to be on a recording but excited.
[00:12] Marcus: Welcome, yeah we'll keep it casual. I'm Marcus, I'll steer a few light questions and keep us on time.
[00:20] Samir: Hi all. Hi Priya. We've done a couple internal rehearsals, so hopefully not too many ums.
[00:27] Priya: Awesome. Alright, quick framing: we're capturing BlueNova's story about shipping embeddings-driven search and a summarization feature using Redwood. This is not a technical deep dive, feel free to keep answers approachable for product folks.
[00:41] Lucia: Sounds great. We can always add a technical appendix later.
[00:45] Marcus: First question — can you tell us briefly why you looked for a new inference platform back in Q2? What wasn't working?
[00:53] Emma: Sure. So, we were running on a mix of self-hosted endpoints and a big cloud vendor — costs got out of hand and latency was inconsistent. For our internal search, 400–600ms was fine but for the customer-facing chat and summarize, spikes killed the UX. Also managing model versions across teams was becoming a nightmare.
[01:12] Samir: And to add, our ops team was spending too much time tuning batching and the KV cache, and we had limited observability into per-route costs.
[01:20] Jordan: When you evaluated Redwood, what were the top criteria? Anything that surprised you?
[01:24] Emma: Predictable cost and an obvious rollout path. We liked the idea of dedicated capacity because our burst patterns are... well, spiky. What surprised me was how much the console made it easy to see token-level spend per route — that was a new angle for us.
[01:40] Lucia: I remember being surprised by the rollout features, like canaries and automatic fallbacks. We accidentally set a canary too narrow the first week — caused a tiny outage, but the fallback kicked in and we didn't notice. That was a relief.
[01:56] Priya: That was the plan, yeah. Also curious — you mentioned latency improvements. Do you have numbers you can share?
[02:03] Samir: Pre-Redwood our p95 for the production summarize endpoint was about 820ms. After moving to Redwood dedicated with the batching recommendations we got, the p95 dropped to ~210–240ms for typical seq lengths. CPU/GPU utilization was more predictable too, so cost per 1k tokens dropped around 28% in the first two months.
[02:23] Emma: Important to call out that's a combination of better batching, model variant selection, and the prefix cache for repeated context. Not just raw hardware.
[02:33] Marcus: Great quote material. On the security side — several customers ask about SOC 2, KMS, VPC. What was your ask and how did Redwood respond?
[02:41] Lucia: Our security team insisted on a private deployment for anything with customer PII. Redwood's private option with customer-managed VPC and KMS integration was the win.
[02:50] Samir: We also evaluated other vendors — LargeCloud AI had similar promises but their VPC wiring was more manual and the SLA for dedicated pools was less clear. EdgeServe's toolchain was nice but lacked the same caching and batching controls — that made it harder to reduce unit cost.
[03:08] Emma: The SOC 2 docs and audit logs Redwood provided during procurement helped us move faster. The Security review was a big gating item for us.
[03:16] Priya: Nice. Switching gears to developer experience — how did your engineers find onboarding?
[03:21] Samir: Faster than expected. The SDKs and a starter template got our team to a usable PoC in about three days. We then did a Dedicated pilot with Redwood's SE team helping tune batching and quantization profiles.
[03:34] Emma: One anecdote — we tried a quantized variant for lower-cost inference, it initially regressed on a small set of prompts. Redwood's evaluate/rollback hooks really helped us iterate quickly.
[03:45] Marcus: Good material — we might pull that into the case study. Any memorable surprises during the pilot or early production?
[03:52] Lucia: The amount of savings from reusing context with the prefix cache. We had expected caching to help but the real-world geometry of our user queries made it much more effective.
[04:03] Samir: Also the tracing hooks — being able to trace latency per token back to model version and route helped us find a prompt that was causing a 40% latency jump.
[04:12] Jordan: For the marketing copy, is there a short outcome you can share — like "we saw x improvement" or a customer-facing metric?
[04:18] Emma: Yes — internal metric we track: average support response time for AI-assisted replies dropped from 6.2 minutes down to 1.8 minutes in the quarter after launch; that's partly product changes but mainly the improved model responsiveness and reliability.
[04:33] Marcus: That's a great line. We'll ask you to approve the exact wording in the consent form.
[04:37] Priya: A quick procurement note — you moved from pay-as-you-go to a reserved capacity contract. Did you feel the commit matched your traffic?
[04:45] Samir: We were cautious with the first commit, Redwood helped model our burst capacity with burst windows and we adjusted after month one. The dedicated pool sizing guidance was surprisingly accurate.
[04:57] Lucia: Also worth mentioning — the console's per-route cost attribution helped product decide which features to keep behind a premium plan. That changed our pricing thinking.
[05:08] Marcus: Moving towards the softer side — do you have a favorite story where the tech unlocked a customer outcome?
[05:14] Emma: Sure — a small enterprise customer used our summarization feature to triage support tickets. Before, their triage took hours; after, initial categorization was immediate and human triage time decreased by 65%. They wrote back saying it changed how they staffed support. That was a great customer quote.
[05:32] Marcus: Love that. We'll ask for permission to use the customer quote too.
[05:36] Samir: Happy to share the contact, we'll anonymize if needed.
[05:41] Jordan: On the competitive angle, anything you wish you'd known earlier that might have changed your vendor evaluation?
[05:47] Samir: Know your real latency SLOs — vendors often publish low-latency numbers that don't account for your input shapes or KV cache patterns. Redwood's profile benchmarking helped set realistic expectations.
[06:00] Emma: Also check the model rollback features — they saved us from shipping a model variant that had subtle hallucination regressions on a vertical-specific prompt set.
[06:10] Priya: Good to hear. Logistics for the case study — who should we send the draft to and who signs off from BlueNova?
[06:16] Lucia: I'll be the primary reviewer for product phrasing, Emma gives final sign-off from exec/strategy, and Samir will check any technical claims. For customer quotes, legal will need to vet if we include customer names.
[06:30] Marcus: Noted. We'll route the draft to Lucia and Emma and include Samir on technical claims.
[06:36] Marcus: Anything you want us to avoid saying in public materials?
[06:39] Emma: Don't publish our internal cost per token number, that's sensitive. High level percentages are ok (e.g., ~28% reduction).
[06:47] Jordan: Understood. We'll keep proprietary numbers out.
[06:50] Marcus: Quick pivot — any product feedback for Redwood we've missed that should be passed back to product?
[06:56] Samir: A small UX ask — the console's model diff view when comparing versions could be more explicit about tokenizer changes and effective token counts. That would help planning.
[07:06] Priya: We'll log that as product feedback.
[07:08] Emma: Also request — better exportable audit logs for compliance. We had to stitch together a few sources during our audit.
[07:15] Jordan: Good notes. We'll pass both along.
[07:19] Marcus: Ok, a few marketing-y wrap-up questions: if we asked you for a 1–2 sentence testimonial, what would you say off the cuff?
[07:26] Emma: "BlueNova Labs relies on Redwood Inference to deliver consistent, low-latency LLM features at predictable cost — enabling us to scale product workflows and improve customer response times."
[07:43] Marcus: That is gold. We'll send that as a proposed quote and you can tweak.
[07:48] Lucia: Sounds fine, I'll likely shorten.
[07:51] Jordan: Any do-not-publish items to include in the consent?
[07:54] Samir: Just the internal cost per token and specific contract terms.
[07:58] Marcus: Great. Last thing — what format do you prefer for the case study and podcast release? Short transcript, 600–800 word article, and 10–15 minute edited podcast episode plus 2 social clips?
[08:10] Emma: That sounds right. The team can sign off faster with a shorter draft.
[08:14] Marcus: Perfect. We'll aim for that.
[08:17] [Longer pause while Marcus notes down approvals]
[09:05] Marcus: Quick offscript — Samir, you mentioned a prompt that caused a 40% latency spike. Can you sketch what that looked like and how you mitigated?
[09:13] Samir: Sure, it was a nested chain-of-thought prompt that forced large KV growth per token. We started using prefix caching and moved that route to a model variant optimized for short-term memory.
[09:24] Priya: Nice mitigation. That will be a useful technical sidebar. We won't put too much of that in marketing but can add to a technical appendix.
[09:33] Emma: If you need a technical contact on our side for that appendix, it's Samir.
[09:37] Marcus: Noted.
[09:39] Jordan: Alright, final logistics — approvals: Jordan to send consent form, Marcus to draft the article and show notes, Samir to provide metrics, Lucia to review, Emma to sign off. Anything else?
[09:50] Lucia: If you could also include a plain-English timeline of our migration steps in the draft, that helps our comms team.
[09:57] Marcus: We'll add a timeline section.
[10:01] Emma: One small note — please don't attribute the 65% triage decrease to Redwood alone in the public text; it's a blend of our product flow and improved inference.
[10:11] Marcus: Absolutely. We'll be careful with causal language.
[10:15] [Break in conversation: quick off-mic chatter that got partially transcribed]
[11:02] Jordan: We're running a bit over initial schedule, but any final thoughts or soundbites anyone wants to add on record?
[11:10] Samir: If it's useful: "Redwood reduced friction for our infra team and gave product a faster feedback loop."
[11:18] Lucia: I'll add: "Integrated observability meant we could finally quantify the cost impact of small UX experiments."
[11:27] Emma: And from me: "Redwood's rollback and canary features saved us from a bad release — that reliability matters more than raw latency sometimes."
[11:40] Marcus: Great — we'll capture those as potential pull-quotes.
[11:44] Jordan: Thanks everyone; we'll follow up with the consent doc and the draft in the next week. Any objection to sharing the edited podcast with your comms team before public release?
[11:55] Emma: No objection. Send it to me and legal for a quick check.
[11:59] Marcus: Perfect. We'll aim to send the draft by 2026-11-10.
[12:04] Priya: Thanks all.
[12:06] Samir: Thanks.
[12:07] Lucia: Appreciate it, bye.
[12:09] Marcus: Bye everyone.
[12:12] [Call ends — transcript continues with short outro tag and some filler noise capture]
